```{r setup}
root <- if (dir.exists("R")) "." else ".."
source(file.path(root, "R/params.R"))
source(file.path(root, "R/theme.R"))
source(file.path(root, "R/data.R"))
source(file.path(root, "R/calcs.R"))

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2); library(scales); library(knitr)
})

d        <- load_all_data()
dram_ix  <- dram_index(d$dram)
contribs <- cpi_contributions(d$categories)
timing   <- cpi_timing(contribs, params)
costs    <- channel_costs(d$exposure, params)
sens     <- cpi_sensitivity(params)

# Pull a low/central/high value out of the timing table.
tm <- function(period_prefix, which) {
  timing[[which]][startsWith(timing$period, period_prefix)]
}
f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)

tot_lo <- tm("Total", "low"); tot_c <- tm("Total", "central"); tot_hi <- tm("Total", "high")
y26_lo <- tm("2026", "low");  y26_c <- tm("2026", "central");  y26_hi <- tm("2026", "high")
y27_lo <- tm("2027", "low");  y27_c <- tm("2027", "central");  y27_hi <- tm("2027", "high")

pt_low     <- params$passthrough_year1[["low"]]
pt_central <- params$passthrough_year1[["central"]]
pt_high    <- params$passthrough_year1[["high"]]

fuel_pp      <- fuel_benchmark(params)
fuel_ratio26 <- y26_c / fuel_pp

total_cost_low     <- sum(costs$cost_low)
total_cost_central <- sum(costs$cost_central)
total_cost_high    <- sum(costs$cost_high)
total_cost_gdp_pct <- total_cost_central / params$nz_gdp_nzd_bn * 100

peak_index <- dram_ix %>% filter(quarter_index == max(quarter_index))

cpi_now <- d$macro$value[d$macro$indicator == "Headline CPI inflation (annual)" &
                         d$macro$period == "2026Q2"]
ocr_now <- d$macro$value[d$macro$indicator == "Official Cash Rate"]

# The central case, snapped to the nearest gridline so it sits on a tile.
central_weight_pct <- params$weight_grid[
  which.min(abs(params$weight_grid - sum(contribs$cpi_weight_pct)))]
central_swing_pp <- params$swing_grid[
  which.min(abs(params$swing_grid - tot_c / (sum(contribs$cpi_weight_pct) / 100)))]
```

::: {.callout-important}
## The verdict on inflation

The memory shock adds about **`r f1(tot_c)` percentage points** to New Zealand's
consumer price level in total (range `r f2(tot_lo)`–`r f2(tot_hi)`). Roughly
**`r f1(y26_c)`pp** of that shows up in annual inflation in 2026 and roughly
**`r f1(y27_c)`pp** in 2027, because retailers sell stock bought months earlier.
That is too small to threaten the inflation target, and the Reserve Bank should
look through it. It matters only because it lands on top of a fuel shock that has
already pushed inflation to `r cpi_now`%. From 2028 the risk reverses: if memory
prices crash, as they have at the end of every previous cycle, the effect turns
into a drag.
:::

## In one page {.unnumbered}

Global memory prices have roughly **`r f1(peak_index$index_central/100)`x-ed
since the end of 2025** (range `r f1(peak_index$index_low/100)`x to
`r f1(peak_index$index_high/100)`x). New Zealand produces no memory, so the entire
shock arrives as an import price. Four things follow.

1. **Inflation: small, temporary in its rate, and badly timed.** About
   `r f1(tot_c)`pp on the price level in total, of which roughly `r f2(y26_c)`pp
   lands in 2026 annual inflation (range `r f2(y26_lo)`–`r f2(y26_hi)`). Fuel is
   currently contributing about `r f1(fuel_pp)`pp, so the memory shock's 2026
   effect is around `r sprintf("%.0f%%", fuel_ratio26*100)` of the fuel effect.

2. **Income: a transfer offshore of roughly `r sprintf("NZ$%.1fbn", total_cost_central)` a year**
   (`r f1(total_cost_low)`–`r f1(total_cost_high)`), or about
   **`r sprintf("%.1f%%", total_cost_gdp_pct)` of GDP**. Small. Real. Entirely
   one-way: unlike a dairy price move, there is no New Zealand sector on the
   winning side.

3. **Investment: the important one.** ICT capital has had a *falling* price for
   thirty years. That is a large part of why capital deepening happened at all in a
   country that invests badly. The deflator has now flipped sign. Nothing in the
   inflation number captures this, and it is the channel most likely to still matter
   in 2030.

4. **Distribution: regressive by construction.** The memory-intensive share of a
   device's bill of materials is highest at the bottom of the range. Cheap phones
   and school laptops absorbed the largest proportional hit.

The shock lands on an economy where annual inflation is already **`r cpi_now`%**
and the OCR is **`r ocr_now`%**. That context does more work in this note than
any of the memory numbers.

::: {.callout-note}
## What this note is, and is not

This is a framework note with orders of magnitude attached, written to be
checkable rather than precise. There is no econometrics in it, deliberately: the
underlying price series has four quarterly observations and there is no New
Zealand micro data on device prices in the public domain. A regression on that
would be a decoration, not a finding.

Every number is either sourced in @sec-sources or declared an assumption in
`R/params.R`. Where a number is an assumption, it carries a range, and the range
is wide. Several of the New Zealand quantities — CPI basket weights for device
categories, spend bases by channel — are **estimates the author could not verify
against Stats NZ directly** and should be replaced with the published series
before this note is used for anything consequential. @sec-falsify says what
would change the conclusions.

**Data are as at 25 August 2026.** The September 2026 quarter CPI, released
since, is not incorporated; its computing equipment sub-index is the first direct
test of the estimates here.
:::

## The shock itself

Memory is not behaving like a component price. It is behaving like a commodity in
a squeeze, because that is what it has become: three suppliers, capacity
reallocated to high-bandwidth memory for AI accelerators, and a demand curve that
for hyperscalers is close to vertical.

```{r fig-dram}
#| label: fig-dram
#| fig-cap: "Conventional DRAM contract prices, quarter-on-quarter. The 2026Q3 figure is a forecast."

ggplot(d$dram %>% filter(quarter_index > 0),
       aes(x = quarter, y = qoq_central_pct, fill = status)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = qoq_low_pct, ymax = qoq_high_pct),
                width = 0.15, colour = pal[["neutral"]]) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("+%.0f%%", qoq_central_pct)),
            vjust = -1.6, size = 3.4, colour = pal[["neutral"]]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(actual = pal[["actual"]], forecast = pal[["forecast"]])) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(scale = 1), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  labs(title = "Three quarters that repriced a commodity input",
       subtitle = "Quarter-on-quarter change in conventional DRAM contract prices",
       x = NULL, y = "QoQ change",
       caption = wrap_cap(paste("Source: TrendForce, via trade press.",
                                "Bars show the central estimate; whiskers show the reported range."))) +
  theme_note()
```

The quarterly rates are decelerating, which is being read in some coverage as the
shock ending. It is not. Decelerating growth in a price level is still a rising
price level, and the compounding is what matters:

```{r fig-index}
#| label: fig-index
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative DRAM contract price level, 2025Q4 = 100."

ggplot(dram_ix, aes(x = quarter_index, y = index_central)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = index_low, ymax = index_high),
              fill = pal[["light"]], alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(colour = pal[["actual"]], linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = pal[["actual"]], size = 2.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", colour = pal[["neutral"]]) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f", index_central)),
            vjust = -1.1, hjust = 1.15, size = 3.4, colour = pal[["neutral"]]) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = dram_ix$quarter_index, labels = dram_ix$quarter) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "The deceleration is not a reversal",
       subtitle = "Cumulative contract price index, 2025Q4 = 100. Shaded band is the reported range.",
       x = NULL, y = "Index",
       caption = wrap_cap(paste("Derived by compounding the quarterly changes in Figure 1.",
                                "Compounding a range widens it fast: treat the endpoint as an order of magnitude."))) +
  theme_note()
```

Two features of this shock matter more for New Zealand than its size.

**It is long.** Samsung told its second-quarter 2026 call that incremental supply
is unlikely before 2028 and that constraints tighten in 2027. Micron puts
meaningful output from new US and Singapore capacity at mid-2027 at the earliest.
A shock that resolves in two quarters is noise; a shock that resolves in eight is
a planning parameter.

**It is bimodal.** Memory is the most reliably cyclical market in manufacturing,
and every previous squeeze has ended in a glut. The distribution of 2028 outcomes
is not a bell curve around today's price — it is a spike at "still tight" and a
spike at "collapsed", with not much in between. Anyone presenting a single
central path for memory prices in 2028, this note included, is presenting the
mean of a distribution with no mass at the mean. Plan for both tails.

## Five channels into New Zealand

New Zealand's exposure is simple to characterise because the country's position
is simple: a small, distant, wholly import-dependent consumer of a good whose
price is set elsewhere, with no offsetting export interest. Taiwan and Korea are
experiencing this as a terms-of-trade boom. New Zealand is on the other side of
that trade with nothing to hedge it.

### Channel 1: consumer prices

The calculation has two steps: how much the shock adds to the price level in
total, and when that shows up in annual inflation.

**Step 1: the total.** A category's contribution is its CPI weight times its
price swing.

```{r tbl-contrib}
#| label: tbl-contrib
contribs %>%
  transmute(
    Category = category,
    `CPI weight (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", cpi_weight_pct),
    `Trend (%/yr)` = sprintf("%+.0f", trend_annual_pct),
    `Under shock (%/yr)` = sprintf("%+.0f", shock_annual_central_pct),
    `Swing (pp)` = sprintf("%.0f", swing_central),
    `Contribution (pp)` = sprintf("%.2f", contrib_central)
  ) %>%
  bind_rows(tibble(
    Category = "**Total**",
    `CPI weight (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", sum(contribs$cpi_weight_pct)),
    `Trend (%/yr)` = "", `Under shock (%/yr)` = "", `Swing (pp)` = "",
    `Contribution (pp)` = sprintf("**%.2f**", tot_c)
  )) %>%
  kable(align = "lrrrrr",
        caption = "Total contribution to the CPI price level once fully passed through, central case. Weights are author estimates, not Stats NZ published weights.")
```

The **swing** is the honest way to frame this, and it is why the number is larger
than it looks. Computing equipment has not been a source of inflation in living
memory; it has been a quiet, persistent source of *dis*inflation, running perhaps
3–5% below zero every year on a quality-adjusted basis. Gartner's estimate of a
17% rise in PC prices in 2026 is therefore not a 17-point event in the index. It
is a **21-point** event, because the counterfactual was negative. The same logic
applies, more weakly, to phones and audio-visual gear.

**Step 2: the timing.** New Zealand retail sells inventory bought forward, often
two or three quarters ahead. This note assumes
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", pt_central*100)` of the cost increase reaches shelves in the
first year (range `r sprintf("%.0f%%", pt_low*100)`–`r sprintf("%.0f%%", pt_high*100)`)
and the rest the year after:

```{r tbl-timing}
#| label: tbl-timing
timing %>%
  transmute(
    ` ` = period,
    `Central (pp)` = f2(central),
    `Range (pp)` = paste(f2(low), "to", f2(high))
  ) %>%
  kable(align = "lrr",
        caption = "When the shock shows up. The 2026 and 2027 rows always sum to the total, so their ranges move in opposite directions and should not be added together.")
```

So the number to quote for any single year's inflation is about
**`r f1(y26_c)`pp in 2026**, not the `r f1(tot_c)`pp total. Two caveats on the
2027 row. It covers only the spill-over from the 2026 repricing; if memory prices
keep rising through 2027, as suppliers are guiding, 2027 carries a fresh increment
on top. And it would be visible but never dramatic in any single quarterly print.

The **weight** is where this note is most exposed. New Zealand's published CPI
expenditure weights for these categories were not accessible when this was
written, and the figures in @tbl-contrib are estimates from comparable
advanced-economy baskets. So rather than defend a point estimate, here is the
whole parameter space for the total:

```{r fig-sens}
#| label: fig-sens
#| fig-cap: "Total CPI contribution across the plausible parameter space. The marked point is this note's central case."

ggplot(sens, aes(x = swing_pp, y = weight_pct, fill = contribution_pp)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", contribution_pp)), size = 2.6, colour = "grey20") +
  annotate("point", x = central_swing_pp, y = central_weight_pct,
           shape = 21, size = 7, stroke = 1.4, colour = pal[["accent"]], fill = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = pal[["forecast"]], guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = params$swing_grid) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = params$weight_grid, labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  labs(title = "The answer is small across the whole parameter space",
       subtitle = "Total contribution to the CPI price level, 2026 and 2027 combined (percentage points)",
       x = "Average price swing vs trend (percentage points)",
       y = "Total CPI weight of affected categories (%)",
       caption = wrap_cap(paste("Read this as the range of defensible answers, not as a probability surface.",
                                "Even the top-right corner is under 0.7pp, and that is spread over two years."))) +
  theme_note() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

This is the most useful thing in the note. It says that **no reasonable choice of
parameters makes the memory shock a first-order inflation event for New Zealand.**
Even the extreme corner of the grid is under 0.7pp in total, and pass-through
spreads that across two years. If someone tells you memory prices are going to
derail the inflation target on their own, they are wrong on the arithmetic, and
the arithmetic is not hard.

Two further qualifications.

**Measured CPI will understate the welfare loss.** The dominant manufacturer
response to a component cost spike is not a price rise but a specification cut:
the same laptop at the same price with 8GB instead of 16GB. Statistics New
Zealand quality-adjusts this category, so in principle a spec cut is recorded as
a price increase. In practice, hedonic models fitted over two decades of falling
memory prices are being asked to extrapolate in a direction the training period
never contained. The bias is one-directional: the figures above are what CPI is
likely to *show*, and the cost-of-living hit households experience is somewhat
larger, by an amount this note does not estimate.

**The exchange rate can swamp all of this.** Every item here is USD-priced. A 10%
move in NZD/USD is worth more to landed device costs than a full quarter of DRAM
contract inflation. Any forecast of New Zealand device prices is mostly a currency
forecast wearing a semiconductor costume.

### Channel 2: the import bill

```{r fig-channels}
#| label: fig-channels
#| fig-cap: "Estimated annual cost by channel, before behavioural response."
#| fig-height: 3.4

costs %>%
  mutate(channel = factor(channel, levels = rev(channel))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = channel, x = cost_central)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = cost_low, xend = cost_high, yend = channel),
               colour = pal[["light"]], linewidth = 5, lineend = "round") +
  geom_point(colour = pal[["actual"]], size = 3.6) +
  geom_text(aes(x = cost_high, label = sprintf("$%.2fbn", cost_central)),
            hjust = -0.35, size = 3.2, colour = pal[["neutral"]]) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(prefix = "NZ$", suffix = "bn"),
                     limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.30))) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) gsub(" \\(", "\n(", x)) +
  labs(title = "Where the money goes",
       subtitle = "Additional annual cost at steady state, NZ$ billion",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = wrap_cap(paste(
         "Grey bars show the low-high range; the dot is the central case.",
         "Spend bases are author estimates scaled from trade aggregates.",
         "Confidence is 'low' for the cloud and public sector lines."))) +
  theme_note() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 1, size = 9))
```

Roughly **`r sprintf("NZ$%.1fbn", total_cost_central)` a year**, or
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", total_cost_gdp_pct)` of GDP, at steady state and before
anyone changes their behaviour. For scale: a 20% swing in dairy export prices
moves national income by something closer to NZ$5bn on a roughly NZ$25bn export
base. The memory shock is a fraction of a bad dairy season. It is not a
macroeconomic event.

Two framings are worth keeping distinct, because they get confused constantly.
The **import bill** will rise by less than this, because people will buy fewer and
cheaper devices — quantity adjusts. The **welfare loss** is close to the full
figure regardless, because it shows up as the devices not bought and the
capability not acquired. If you are watching the trade balance you will
under-read this shock; the adjustment hides in volumes.

### Channel 3: the price of capital deepening {#sec-capital}

This is the channel that deserves the attention it will not get.

For thirty years, ICT has been the only major capital good with a persistently
negative deflator. That single fact does an enormous amount of work in growth
accounting: it is why firms in low-investment economies nonetheless accumulated
computing capital, because the same nominal budget bought more real capital every
year without anyone deciding anything. New Zealand, which invests poorly by the
standards of its peers and has had flat measured labour productivity for years,
has been a quiet beneficiary of that automatic deepening.

The deflator has flipped. A firm with a fixed nominal IT budget now buys *less*
real capital each year, not more. The mechanical response — already visible in
enterprise purchasing — is to extend refresh cycles: four years to five, five to
six. That looks like prudent cost management on any one balance sheet. In
aggregate it is a reduction in the rate of capital deepening, and it will show up
in productivity statistics with a lag long enough that nobody will attribute it
correctly.

The size is not knowable from public data, and this note does not pretend to
estimate it. The point is structural: **a 15% rise in the price of ICT capital is
a larger event for New Zealand's growth path than a 0.2pp rise in annual CPI, and
only one of them will be discussed.**

### Channel 4: cloud and the data centre pipeline

New Zealand is a net importer of cloud. Microsoft's Auckland region opened in
December 2024; AWS committed NZ$7.5bn and went live in September 2025; Invest New
Zealand is chasing NZ$25–30bn of data centre investment over five years. None of
that changes the direction of the trade — hosting capacity being physically here
does not make the compute domestically produced.

So the cloud channel is close to unambiguous. AWS raised GPU instance prices 15%
in January 2026, the first increase in the company's history, and lifted EC2
Capacity Blocks around 20% in July. Analyst guidance to enterprises is to budget
10–15% cloud cost growth through 2026–27 on cost pass-through alone. Every one of
those points is imported inflation for a New Zealand buyer, and the effect is
larger for memory-intensive services — databases, caching, analytics — than for
general compute. If you run a New Zealand SaaS business, your COGS line is the
place this shock will find you first.

The **build side** is genuinely ambiguous, and should be presented that way.
Memory inflation raises capex per megawatt substantially for AI-configured
capacity, which pushes marginal projects out — and New Zealand is a marginal
region on almost every dimension that matters: small domestic demand, long
latency to everywhere, no cost advantage in power. There is already evidence of
projects being reconsidered: Microsoft let an Overseas Investment Office consent
lapse at Whenuapai, and AWS wrote off NZ$44.9m on an abandoned Westgate site.
Neither is attributable to memory prices, and it would be sloppy to claim
otherwise. But the same cost pressure also pushes workloads *out* of on-premise
and into cloud — AWS has said as much — which raises utilisation of capacity
already built. Whether New Zealand nets out ahead depends on which effect
dominates, and nothing in the public data resolves it.

The honest forward indicator is not a price series. It is the consent register:
watch whether OIO applications for data centre sites are lodged, extended, or
allowed to lapse over the next four quarters.

### Channel 5: fiscal and distributional

**Fiscal.** Government IT budgets are set in nominal terms against fixed
baselines. A 10–15% increase in cloud contract costs and a similar rise in device
fleet replacement is, arithmetically, a real cut to whatever else those agencies
buy. Health, education and justice all run large device fleets on multi-year
refresh cycles, and several of those cycles fall due inside the shock window. The
risk is not a headline fiscal number; it is a set of deferred refreshes that
convert into service quality and security exposure two or three years out.

**Distributional.** The incidence is regressive, and unusually clearly so.
Memory is a larger share of the bill of materials at the bottom of the device
range than at the top, so the proportional cost increase is largest for the
cheapest goods: reported production cost increases of 20–30% for sub-US$200
phones against 10–15% for mid and high-end devices. Globally, sales of
sub-US$100 phones fell 64% year on year, with some manufacturers withdrawing from
the segment. For New Zealand this reads directly onto digital inclusion — the
entry-level device is the one that got repriced hardest, and household connection
and device access are already the binding constraint for the households furthest
from the digital economy. Any programme with a device-provision component should
be re-costed now rather than discovering the gap at procurement.

## What it means for monetary policy

The verdict at the top of this note in one line: **small, look through it, but
mind the company it keeps.** The rest of this section explains the last clause.

The textbook answer is easy and correct as far as it goes: this is a **relative
price shock, not an inflation shock**. It raises the price of one category of
goods against everything else. A flexible inflation targeter should look through
the first-round effect and respond only if inflation expectations move. Nothing
in @fig-sens argues otherwise; the numbers are simply too small.

The complication is context, not size. Annual inflation was `r cpi_now`% in the
June 2026 quarter, above the 1–3% band, driven overwhelmingly by fuel. The OCR
sits at `r ocr_now`%. The Reserve Bank is already looking through one supply
shock. The relevant question is not "how large is the memory shock" — it is
small — but "**how many simultaneous look-throughs does a central bank get before
the public stops distinguishing between a relative price shock and
inflation?**" That is a question about credibility, not arithmetic. It is why a
shock worth about `r f1(y26_c)`pp a year deserves a sentence in 2026 monetary
policy communication when the same shock in 2019 would not have.

Three further observations.

**Its persistence cuts both ways.** Unlike an oil spike, this does not mean-revert
on a known schedule; supply relief is not expected before 2028. A shock that
delivers a small positive contribution for eight consecutive quarters is harder to
communicate as transitory than one large quarter that visibly unwinds — even
though, in strict terms, a slow level shift is exactly what a central bank should
ignore.

**It arrives in tradables, where the Bank has least traction.** June 2026
tradables inflation was 4.9% against non-tradables at 3.4%. Tightening domestic
conditions to offset an imported component price is a poor trade; the memory
shock is best treated as a level shift in the tradables series to be looked
through, not leaned against.

**The tail risk is disinflationary.** If 2027–28 capacity lands into softening AI
demand, memory prices do not gently normalise — they collapse, and the device
deflation resumes with force. The risk to a 2028 inflation forecast built on
today's memory prices is meaningfully skewed to the downside. This is the least
discussed and most likely-to-embarrass feature of the whole episode.

## What would change these conclusions {#sec-falsify}

Stating this properly is the price of publishing estimates built on assumptions.

| If this turned out to be true | Then |
|---|---|
| Published Stats NZ weights for these categories are materially above ~2.6% of the basket | The CPI contribution rises above the grid in @fig-sens; re-run with real weights |
| The September 2026 quarter computing equipment index is still falling | Pass-through is slower or smaller than assumed; the 2026 figure is too high |
| NZD/USD falls 15%+ | The currency effect dominates the memory effect entirely; this note becomes a footnote to an exchange rate story |
| Memory prices fall QoQ in any quarter before 2027Q2 | The squeeze is breaking early; treat the whole thing as a completed cycle and expect resumed deflation |
| Hedonic adjustment is found to be absorbing spec cuts fully | The measured-vs-experienced gap in Channel 1 disappears and CPI is the right measure after all |
| Data centre OIO consents lapse or are withdrawn over the next four quarters | Channel 4 resolves negative for New Zealand; the build-side ambiguity closes the wrong way |
| Enterprise refresh cycles are observed lengthening in survey data | Channel 3 is confirmed and becomes the main story; escalate it accordingly |

The single most valuable thing anyone could do to improve this note costs about
an hour: pull the actual CPI expenditure weights and the computing equipment
sub-index (including the September 2026 quarter) from Stats NZ Infoshare and
replace the estimates in `data/consumer_categories.csv`. Everything downstream
recalculates.

## Provenance {#sec-sources}

Every input, with its tier. Nothing in this note is sourced to a number that does
not appear below. URLs and access dates are in `data/sources.csv`.

```{r tbl-sources}
#| label: tbl-sources
d$sources %>%
  mutate(tier = factor(tier, levels = source_tiers)) %>%
  arrange(tier, source_id) %>%
  transmute(
    Tier = as.character(tier),
    Claim = claim,
    Value = value,
    Source = source
  ) %>%
  kable(caption = "Input provenance. 'assumption' means the author chose it within a declared range; 'weak' means a secondary aggregator that was not independently verified.")
```

**Tiers.** *official* — national statistical agency or central bank.
*industry* — named analyst house (TrendForce, Gartner, IDC, Counterpoint) or
company statement, reached via trade press rather than the primary document.
*media* — reported, single source. *weak* — trade aggregator or secondary
compilation, not independently verified. *assumption* — the author's, with a
range, documented in `R/params.R`.

**A note on access.** Stats NZ, Trading Economics, OEC and CRAN were all
unreachable from the environment this was written in. Official New Zealand
figures here come from search-indexed summaries of Stats NZ and RBNZ releases
rather than from the releases themselves, and the trade aggregates are secondary.
That is a real limitation and is why the New Zealand-specific quantities carry
the widest ranges in the note.

**Revision history.** First drafted 25 August 2026. Revised 2 November 2026: the
pass-through assumption, previously stated in the text but not applied, now
drives a 2026/2027 split of the CPI effect; the verdict is stated once, up front.
